metaTitle: How Emerge works: satellites, a fair fire record and a next-day model
metaDescription: Which data each NASA satellite gives, how 25 years of MODIS and VIIRS fire detections become one fair record, how the next-day risk model works, how it compares and where it falls short.
title: How Emerge works
lead: Emerge reads fire detections from five satellites, puts the older and the newer instrument on one scale, and ranks where new fires are most likely tomorrow. Every number on this page is read from the same files the app uses.

sources.title: What each satellite and source gives us
sources.body: Two instruments look for fires from orbit. MODIS has flown since 2000 and sees the ground in pixels about 1 km wide. VIIRS has flown since 2012 with pixels of 375 m, so it also catches smaller and cooler fires. NASA FIRMS publishes the detections of both.
sources.timelineCaption: When each instrument is in the record
sources.snppNote: 375 m, from January 2012; new data stopped about 2 November 2026
sources.noaa20Note: 375 m, from 2018; history and test labels for the model
sources.noaa21Note: 375 m, recent fires only, no yearly files yet
sources.pixelCaption: Drawn to scale. One MODIS pixel covers about seven VIIRS pixels.
sources.matrixTitle: What feeds the model, and what is only on the map
sources.recordModisNote: 1 km, 2000 on, converted to VIIRS level
sources.recordNoaa20Note: a second VIIRS to check the first
sources.modelFwiNote: the fire weather index and its six parts, built from temperature, humidity, wind and rain
sources.modelFiresNote: earlier years in each square, and fires nearby in the last days of data
sources.modelLandNote: the main land class of each square: forest, shrub and grass, or farmland
sources.modelCalendarNote: the season and the latitude of each square
sources.mapNote: Shown so you can see the conditions. The model does not read them.

record.title: How the fair record is built
record.body: When VIIRS joined in 2012, the number of fires seen worldwide jumped. Fires did not suddenly multiply: the new instrument sees more of them. Year after year, S-NPP finds about {ratio} times as many fire cell-days as MODIS.
record.cellDay: A fire cell-day counts a small ground cell once for each day it shows a detection, so a big fire seen by many pixels still counts once per cell and day.
record.chartCaption: Fire cell-days worldwide, millions per year
record.agreement: Two VIIRS satellites agree within about {pct} ({from} to {to}). The step is the instrument, not the fires.
record.stepsTitle: Bringing MODIS years up to VIIRS level
record.step1: Every month of every 0.25° cell is placed in a group by three keys.
record.step2: In each group, compare what VIIRS and MODIS saw in the same months, {months}, across {countries} countries.
record.step3: Groups with little fire are pulled towards their country's ratio, and then the world's, so one odd month cannot swing them.
record.step4: Where MODIS saw nothing in a month, a small background value is added, because VIIRS would often have seen fire there.
record.step5: Every converted month carries an error range, and the calendar marks values before February 2012 as estimated.
record.testTitle: Tested on years it never saw
record.statForward: Typical monthly error worldwide, trained on 2012 to 2018, tested on 2019 to 2022
record.statReverse: The same, trained on 2016 to 2022, tested backwards on 2012 to 2015
record.statCountry: Median monthly error per country, {n} countries scored
record.statCountryRange: {large} in the third that burns most, {small} in the third that burns least
record.statRange: How often a 90% range held the true value, cell by cell
record.errorNote: Error here is nRMSE: the size of the monthly errors compared with the average monthly value. Small countries with little fire have large relative errors, and the app shows their wider ranges.

model.title: How the next-day model works
model.body: Every land square of {grid}° (about 28 km) gets a chance that a new fire is detected in it tomorrow. Inside each region the squares are then ranked, and the chance sets the level shown on the map.
model.inPlaceNote: the forecast date and the square
model.fWeatherNote: the index, its six parts, and the index in forest squares
model.fHistoryNote: share of earlier years with fire here in this month, fire last year, days since the last fire
model.fNearbyNote: a fire in the square or its eight neighbours in the last three days of data
model.fLandNote: forest, shrub and grass, farmland, or unknown
model.fSeasonNote: the month on a circle, so December sits next to January
model.lgbmNote: Many small decision trees, each one correcting the mistakes of the trees before it. The result is a chance from 0 to 1 for each square and day.
model.outRankNote: the top squares of each region and day are the ones to watch
model.timingTitle: Only what would have been known in time
model.timingBody: A forecast for day D uses fire detections up to the end of day D-2, the NASA fire-weather forecast issued three days before D, and the NOAA weather forecast issued two days before D. Nothing from day D or the day before goes in.
model.splitTitle: Trained, tuned and tested on different years
model.fForecastNote: highest temperature, lowest humidity, wind and gusts, rain on the day and the next three days, days since rain
model.fPeopleNote: how many people live in the square, how many roads cross it, how much of it is built up

compare.title: How it compares
compare.body: The test asks a firefighter's question: if you could watch only five squares in each region tomorrow, how many of the new fires would land in them? On every test day of {year}, each method ranks the same forest and wildland squares, and we count the new fires its top 5 caught.
compare.chartCaption: Share of new fires caught in the top 5 squares per region and day, {year}
compare.scopeDetail: {days} region-days with new fires, {fires} new fires
compare.headline: Worldwide in {year} the model caught {ratio} times as many new fires as NASA's fire-weather index: {model} against {fwi}.
compare.randomNote: Random already catches {random} in Europe, because many regions there have few squares. That is why beating the baselines matters more than the percentage itself.
compare.hitRate: The model caught at least one new fire on {europe} of the region-days with fire in Europe, and {world} worldwide.
compare.gainBody: We redrew the year {draws} times from whole weeks and recomputed the gain each time. Each bar is the 95% range of the gain in percentage points. A claim is allowed only when the whole range is above zero.
compare.weekBody: For 3 to 8 days ahead the previous model version, version 2, runs on older fire data and longer-range weather. Worldwide it stays above history at every lead, and the gap narrows. This setup was chosen after seeing {year}, so it still needs a fresh test period.
compare.weekCaption: World, share of new fires caught, by days ahead
compare.logBody: Each published outlook is scored against what the satellites then saw. The log has just started, so it shows the method working, not a result yet.
compare.publishedTitle: Published models: context, not a ranking
compare.publishedBody: Other teams report higher or lower percentages, but each one measures something different, on different data. They cannot go on the chart above.
compare.wispMeasure: next-day fire clusters placed within 5 km
compare.wispNote: The closest task to ours: next-day active fires on a 375 m grid from 48 hours of inputs.
compare.ororaNote: A strict measure that does not reward the millions of easy no-fire squares. Their 37 inputs are a checklist for ours.
compare.mesogeosNote: Measured on test sets with fixed shares of fire and no-fire samples, built around large fires. Real days are almost all no-fire, so it does not carry over.
compare.ecmwfNote: Open source. We plan to score it on the same squares and days as a third baseline.
compare.proofLink: Every score, slice and check is on the How we know page.
compare.versus: Version 3, now on the map, replaced version 2 after a single test on these same days: it caught {capture} of new fires worldwide against {previousCapture}, and of the 1,000 squares it ranked highest each day, {alarms} had a new fire against {previousAlarms}, so fewer false alarms.

limits.title: Limits, said plainly
limits.inputs: Plant greenness and soil moisture were tested for version 3 and did not improve it, so they are not used; holidays are not used yet. Population and roads stand in for people, who start most fires in Europe; they do not show where or when someone lights one.
limits.grid: Squares are about 28 km across. A smaller area on the map still gets its whole square's value.
limits.city: Some city squares were overstated by version 2: Sofia's came out about {n} times its own history. This has not been re-measured for version 3.
limits.calibration: Low chances are too low. In Europe's lowest band, on days with fire in the region, the model said {predicted} on average and {observed} of those squares had a new fire.
limits.continuing: For fires that are already burning, earlier-years history does better than the model: {history} against {model} in Europe.
limits.testYear: Version 3 was tested once, on January to October {year}, after it was frozen. 2025 had been the test year of version 2; for version 3 it was used to choose inputs and settings, so it is not a test of this version.
limits.notOfficial: This is a research prototype. It is not an official warning and gives no orders to anyone.
